rmt-2016-geo-01.title: Angle bisector and Pythagoras
rmt-2016-geo-01.body:
By the angle bisector theorem $\frac{BE}{EC}=\frac{AB}{AC}=\frac32$, so $BE=9$, $EC=6$. Let $BD=x$. Then $AD^2=144-x^2=64-(15-x)^2$, so $144=64-225+30x$, $x=\frac{305}{30}=\frac{61}6$. Hence $DE=\frac{61}6-9=\frac76$.

**Answer: $\frac76$**

rmt-2016-geo-03.title: Symmetric placement
rmt-2016-geo-03.body:
The largest square has its four vertices on four different edges, with center at the cube's center. By symmetry each vertex lies at the same distance $x$ from a vertex of the cube along its edge. Take the vertices $P_1=(x,0,0)$, $P_2=(0,1,x)$, $P_3=(1-x,1,1)$, $P_4=(1,0,1-x)$. Then $P_1P_2^2=x^2+1+x^2=2x^2+1$ and $P_2P_3^2=(1-x)^2+0+(1-x)^2=2(1-x)^2$. For a square the two must be equal: $2x^2+1=2-4x+2x^2$, so $x=\frac14$ and the side squared is $2\cdot\frac1{16}+1=\frac98$ (one checks $P_3P_4^2=P_4P_1^2=\frac98$ and the diagonals $P_1P_3^2=P_2P_4^2=\frac94$, as required for a square). So the square $\left(\frac14,0,0\right)$, $\left(0,1,\frac14\right)$, $\left(\frac34,1,1\right)$, $\left(1,0,\frac34\right)$ has area $\frac98$, and this is the largest such square.

**Answer: $\frac98$**

rmt-2016-geo-04.title: Equilateral triangle of centers
rmt-2016-geo-04.body:
Let the small radius be $r$. The centers form an equilateral triangle of side $2r$ whose circumcenter is the center $O$ of the large circle, so $OP=\frac{2r}{\sqrt3}$ for each center $P$. The small circle is tangent internally to the large one, so $OP+r=1$: $r\left(1+\frac2{\sqrt3}\right)=1$, $r=\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt3+2}=\sqrt3(2-\sqrt3)=2\sqrt3-3$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt3-3$**

rmt-2016-geo-05.title: Hexagonal lattice
rmt-2016-geo-05.body:
The densest packing is the hexagonal lattice: each circle is tangent to six others. With radius $1$, the centers form a lattice of equilateral triangles of side $2$. Each such triangle has area $\sqrt3$ and contains angular sectors of three circles totaling $\frac12$ of one disc, i.e. area $\frac\pi2$. So the density is $\frac{\pi/2}{\sqrt3}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}=\frac{\pi\sqrt3}6\approx0.9069$.

**Answer: $\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}$**

rmt-2016-geo-07.title: Set up with the half-angle
rmt-2016-geo-07.body:
Let the sector's apex be $A$ and its angle be $\theta=\arcsin\frac13$, with axis along the $x$-axis. The square has side $s$; two vertices lie on the two straight edges (at $x=x_0$, $y=\pm\frac s2$, so $\tan\frac\theta2=\frac{s/2}{x_0}$, i.e. $x_0=\frac s2\cot\frac\theta2$) and two vertices lie on the arc ($x=x_0+s$, $y=\pm\frac s2$, at distance $1$ from $A$). So $\left(\frac s2\cot\frac\theta2+s\right)^2+\left(\frac s2\right)^2=1$. Since $\cos\theta=\frac{2\sqrt2}3$, $\cot\frac\theta2=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=3+2\sqrt2$. Then $s^2\left[\left(\frac{3+2\sqrt2}2+1\right)^2+\frac14\right]=1$, i.e. $s^2\left[\frac{(5+2\sqrt2)^2+1}4\right]=s^2\cdot\frac{34+20\sqrt2}4=1$. So $s^2=\frac4{34+20\sqrt2}=\frac{2}{17+10\sqrt2}=\frac{2(17-10\sqrt2)}{289-200}=\frac{34-20\sqrt2}{89}$.

**Answer: $\frac{34-20\sqrt2}{89}$**

rmt-2016-geo-08.title: Rectangles plus sectors
rmt-2016-geo-08.body:
On each straight side she paints a rectangle of width $1$ and length equal to the side, with total area $2016\cdot1$. At each vertex she paints a circular sector of radius $1$ whose angle is the exterior (turning) angle. For a closed convex curve the turning angles add to $2\pi$, so the sectors together make a full unit disc of area $\pi$. The pieces do not overlap. Total area $2016+\pi$.

**Answer: $2016+\pi$**
